title: Transition Metals and Complex Ions
seo_title: Year 13 A Level Chemistry: Transition Metals Worksheets
standard_text: Properties of transition metals, complex ions and ligands, shapes and co-ordination numbers, colour, variable oxidation states, catalysts, reactions of ions in aqueous solution and redox titrations.
meta_desc: Free Year 13 A level chemistry worksheets on transition metals: complex ions, ligands, co-ordination numbers, shapes, colours, catalysts and redox titrations with manganate(VII) and dichromate(VI). 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Ligands donate lone pairs to the metal ion.
body_html:
How to think about it

A transition metal forms at least one stable ion with a partly filled d sub-shell. Ligands form co-ordinate bonds to the metal ion; six small ligands give an octahedral complex, four Cl⁻ give tetrahedral, Ag(NH₃)₂⁺ is linear and cisplatin is square planar.

Complexes are coloured because d electrons absorb visible light. In titrations MnO₄⁻ (purple → colourless) reacts with Fe²⁺ in a 1 : 5 ratio.

Example

Oxidation state of Fe in [Fe(CN)₆]³⁻?

6 × (−1) + x = −3

Answer: +3

Example

20.0 cm³ of 0.020 mol dm⁻³ KMnO₄ reacts with Fe²⁺. n(Fe²⁺)?

n(MnO₄⁻) = 4.0 × 10⁻⁴

× 5

Answer: 2.0 × 10⁻³ mol

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting the charges on ligands such as Cl⁻ and CN⁻.
  • Using a 1 : 1 ratio in redox titrations.
  • Saying the colour seen is the colour absorbed.

faq.q: Why are transition metal complexes coloured?
faq.a: Ligands split the d orbitals; electrons absorb visible light to jump between them, and we see the complementary colour.
